claims.text: The baseline is a titanium- and nickel-primary alloy containing at least five elements, each at 5–35 at%.
The baseline alloy can be produced by standard casting or melting routes.
Adding a few atomic percent tungsten will promote precipitation of tungsten-rich phases.
Tungsten addition will produce fine, tungsten-enriched precipitates dispersed in the alloy matrix.
The tungsten-rich precipitates will hinder dislocation motion during elevated-temperature loading.
Hindering dislocation motion through tungsten-rich precipitates will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Hindering dislocation motion through tungsten-rich precipitates will increase elevated-temperature ultimate tensile strength.
Tungsten-rich precipitates will enhance creep resistance.
The tungsten-doped alloy will have greater elevated-temperature strength than the otherwise equivalent tungsten-free baseline.
The tungsten-doped alloy will have lower creep rate or otherwise greater creep resistance than the tungsten-free baseline.
The comparison will use baseline and tungsten-doped batches processed under identical conditions.
Temperature, strain rate, and environment will be held constant during comparative testing.
The hypothesis is restricted to modified alloys that retain at least five elements at 5–35 at% each.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant elevated-temperature mechanical improvement in the tungsten-doped batch relative to the baseline will falsify the hypothesis.
